essentials: RoHS **limits ten hazardous substances** in electrical and electronic equipment sold in the EU.
The limits apply to each **homogeneous material**, not to the product as a whole: 0.1% by weight, and 0.01% for cadmium.
Compliance is part of the **CE marking** and has to be shown in technical documentation.
**Exemptions** allow specific uses for a limited time; they expire unless renewed.

sections.title: Why it exists
text: Electrical and electronic equipment is one of the fastest-growing waste streams. Hazardous substances in it endanger recycling workers and the environment and contaminate recycled material. RoHS removes them at the design stage. It works together with the WEEE Directive, which governs collection and recycling.

Limit
Typical place in a tool

Switches and lamps in older designs
Corrosion protection on screws and housings

after: The four phthalates were added in 2019. They migrate, so a compliant part can be contaminated by contact with a non-compliant one during production or storage.

sections.title: What is covered
points: All electrical and electronic equipment, in eleven categories. **Category 6** is electrical and electronic tools.
Cables and spare parts are covered too.
**Excluded**: among others large-scale stationary industrial tools, and batteries, which have their own regulation.
The limit applies to every **homogeneous material**: a material that cannot be mechanically separated into different materials, such as the insulation of a single wire.

sections.title: Exemptions
text: Annex III lists uses that are exempt because no reliable substitute exists, for example lead as an alloying element in steel, aluminium and copper, and lead in high-melting-temperature solder. Each exemption has an expiry date. Industry can apply for renewal; the exemption stays valid until the Commission decides. A product that relies on an exemption becomes non-compliant when the exemption ends.

sections.title: Who must do what
points: **Manufacturers** (including own-brand sellers) ensure compliance, draw up technical documentation and the EU declaration of conformity, and affix the CE marking.
**Importers** check that the manufacturer has done so and keep the declaration for ten years.

The accepted method is the standard EN IEC 63000: assess how likely each material is to contain a restricted substance and how reliable the supplier is, then collect declarations or test reports accordingly.
after: RoHS is a directive. Germany transposed it in the ElektroStoffV; penalties are national.

terms.text: A material of uniform composition that cannot be mechanically disjointed into different materials.
Electrical and electronic equipment: equipment that depends on electric current or electromagnetic fields to work.
A time-limited permission to use a restricted substance in a defined application.
The harmonised standard for the technical documentation needed to show RoHS compliance.
The directive on waste electrical and electronic equipment, the end-of-life counterpart to RoHS.

related.text: The general chemicals law. Some substances are limited under both; REACH also brings information duties that RoHS does not have.
Batteries are excluded from RoHS and have their own substance limits.
A power tool carries one CE marking that declares conformity with both the machinery rules and RoHS.
Future ecodesign acts can add requirements on substances of concern beyond RoHS.

mistakes.wrong: The limit applies to the weight of the whole product.
mistakes.right: It applies to each homogeneous material, so a tiny non-compliant part makes the product non-compliant.

mistakes.wrong: A supplier's declaration is sufficient proof.
mistakes.right: The documentation must be plausible for the risk. For high-risk materials and less reliable suppliers, test reports are expected.
Exemptions expire. Designs that rely on them need a substitution plan.
They are separate laws with different substances, limits and duties. Both apply.

practice: **Hold a material declaration** for every component, down to homogeneous materials.
**Rank parts by risk** and test the risky ones: cables, grips, solder, alloys, coloured plastics.
**List the exemptions** each product relies on and track their expiry.
**Control changes**: any new material or sub-supplier triggers a new declaration.
**Prevent cross-contamination** with phthalates in the factory.

quiz.q: To what does the 0.1% limit apply?
quiz.why: The concentration is measured in each homogeneous material, such as a wire's insulation or a solder joint.

quiz.q: Which substance has a stricter limit of 0.01%?
quiz.why: Cadmium is limited to 0.01% by weight; the others to 0.1%.

quiz.q: Are the batteries of a cordless tool covered by RoHS?
options: Yes, as part of the tool
No, batteries are covered by the Batteries Regulation
quiz.why: Batteries are excluded from RoHS and regulated separately.

quiz.q: A product uses brass with lead above 0.1% under an Annex III exemption. What must the company watch?
options: The expiry date of the exemption
quiz.why: Exemptions are time-limited. When one ends without renewal, the product no longer complies.

options: Through the CE marking and the EU declaration of conformity
quiz.why: RoHS is a CE-marking directive. There is no official RoHS logo.

quiz.q: Which group of substances was added in 2019?
quiz.why: DEHP, BBP, DBP and DIBP, used as plasticisers in cables and soft plastics.
